*The decorators in `django/views/decorators/` that are a middleware class applied to one view.*

Both replace `CsrfViewMiddleware._reject` with a method that returns `None`, so that a failed check is not an answer, and `_EnsureCsrfCookie` adds a call of `get_token`, which is what makes the middleware's `process_response` send the secret back (`django/views/decorators/csrf.py:_EnsureCsrfToken`, `django/views/decorators/csrf.py:_EnsureCsrfCookie`).

Django's four default error views carry `requires_csrf_token` ([The error views](errors.md)) (`django/views/defaults.py`).
On a site whose chain installs `CsrfViewMiddleware` as well, using `csrf_protect` is, in its docstring's words, "harmless and efficient" (`django/views/decorators/csrf.py`).

The chain's middleware checks the request first, in its `process_view`, and refuses a `"POST"` without a valid token before the decorator's wrapper is called ([The CSRF check: `CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view`](../security/csrf-check.md)) (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view`).

A request it accepts it marks as checked, and the decorator's instance then checks nothing again; its `process_response`, the first of the two to run, sends the secret back where it is due, as when the view has used the token, and leaves the chain's `process_response` nothing to send ([The CSRF secret and its token](../security/csrf-token.md)) (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._accept`, `django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware.process_response`).

`decorator_from_middleware_with_args` returns a function whose arguments are given to the middleware's constructor after the view, and `cache_page` is a small function that calls it with the timeout, the alias and the prefix under the names `CacheMiddleware.__init__` expects (`django/views/decorators/cache.py:cache_page`).
A middleware's first argument is the callable it is to wrap, `get_response`, so the instance believes the view is the rest of the chain (`django/utils/decorators.py:make_middleware_decorator`).

The view is called by the wrapper directly and not through the instance's `get_response` (`django/utils/decorators.py:make_middleware_decorator`, `django/middleware/__init__.py:MiddlewareMixin.__call__`).

If it gives none, the wrapper raises the exception again, and the exception carries on out to the handler, which makes a response of it ([How an exception becomes a response](../handlers/exceptions.md)) (`django/core/handlers/exception.py:convert_exception_to_response`).

As a decorator, a middleware cannot leave to its `process_response` the finishing of what its `process_request` began, as it can in the chain: an answer from its own hooks, or an exception from the view, leaves the wrapper without a call of `process_response` (`django/utils/decorators.py:make_middleware_decorator`).

So for a response with a callable `render` the wrapper does two different things: it calls `process_template_response` straight away, and it registers `process_response` on the response as a callback to be run after rendering (`django/utils/decorators.py:make_middleware_decorator`, `django/template/response.py:SimpleTemplateResponse.add_post_render_callback`).

So for a response with a callable `render` the wrapper does two different things: it calls `process_template_response` straight away, and it registers `process_response` on the response as a callback to be run after rendering (`django/utils/decorators.py:make_middleware_decorator`, `django/template/response.py:SimpleTemplateResponse.add_post_render_callback`).

Between the wrapper's return and the render, the handler runs the chain's own `process_template_response` hooks, on a site that has any ([The centre of the chain](../handlers/view.md#template-responses)) (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler._get_response`).

If the callback returns a response, `render` returns that one in place of the one it rendered, so `process_response` can still replace a response that was not yet rendered, as it could in the chain (`django/template/response.py:SimpleTemplateResponse.render`).
`process_response` is put off until the template has been rendered, as the comment above the callback says (`django/utils/decorators.py:make_middleware_decorator`).

Called in the wrapper, it would be given a response whose content cannot yet be read, for a `SimpleTemplateResponse` refuses its `content` until it has been rendered ([`SimpleTemplateResponse` and `TemplateResponse`](../templates/responses.md#content-refused-before-a-render-contentnotrenderederror)) (`django/template/response.py:SimpleTemplateResponse.content`).
Those the wrapper calls run wherever it is running (`django/utils/decorators.py:make_middleware_decorator`).

Through the same handler, a view that is not a coroutine function gets an ordinary wrapper, which the handler runs on a worker thread, and the hooks and the view run there with it (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler._get_response_async`).

Around a coroutine view, the hooks the wrapper calls are synchronous code running on an event loop: the server's, under an `ASGIHandler`, and under a `WSGIHandler` the one in which `async_to_sync` runs the wrapper (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler._get_response`).

A hook that waits on the network holds up the loop while it waits, as `cache_page`'s hooks do on a cache kept on another server (`django/middleware/cache.py:FetchFromCacheMiddleware.process_request`).

A hook that reaches the database fails outright, since Django refuses a query from a thread whose event loop is running: `cache_page` with the database cache, or `csrf_protect` reading the request's session from the database under `settings.CSRF_USE_SESSIONS`, raises `SynchronousOnlyOperation`, and the client gets a 500 (`django/utils/asyncio.py:async_unsafe`).

Put on a method by `method_decorator`, a decorator made from a middleware makes a middleware for every request, since `method_decorator` applies its decorator again at every call ([Decorating a class: `method_decorator`](method-decorator.md)) (`django/utils/decorators.py:_multi_decorate`).

Some of Django's class-based views are decorated in this way: `LoginView` has `csrf_protect` among the decorators that `method_decorator` puts on its `dispatch`, so each request to a login page constructs a `CsrfViewMiddleware` (`django/contrib/auth/views.py:LoginView`).
